topics.title: Numerical Concept 2: Surds
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: use surds to represent roots that cannot be represented exactly as decimals. (k, u)
manipulate and simplify expressions with surds. (u, s, v/a)

body.text: Opio has a square garden with sides of 1 m. He lays a path straight across it, from one corner to the opposite corner. By Pythagoras’ theorem, the path is √2 m long. A calculator shows 1.4142135… and the digits never stop. In this topic you learn how to work with numbers like √2 exactly, without rounding them.
What is a surd?

The square root of a number is the number that multiplies by itself to give it. For example, √9 = 3 because 3 × 3 = 9. Some square roots are whole numbers or simple fractions, such as √25 = 5 and √(9/16) = 3/4.

Other roots, such as √2, √3 and √5, cannot be written as a fraction. Their decimals go on forever with no repeating pattern. A surd is a root like this, which cannot be written exactly as a fraction or as a terminating or recurring decimal.

A rounded decimal is never exact. For example, 1.414 × 1.414 = 1.999396, which is not 2. When we write √2, the value is exact. So we keep surds in our working and only round at the very end, if a decimal is needed.

body.title: Find surds in paper and diagonals
body.text: Draw a square of side 1 unit, a rectangle 2 units by 1 unit, and a rectangle 4 units by 3 units on squared paper. Use Pythagoras’ theorem to find the length of each diagonal. Which diagonals are surds and which are whole numbers? Then take a sheet of A4 paper, measure its long and short sides, and divide the long side by the short side. Fold the sheet in half and repeat. Compare your answers with √2 ≈ 1.414 and discuss what you notice.
Rules for surds
These rules work for any positive numbers a and b.

body.speech: root a times root b equals root of a b
root a over root b equals the root of a over b
root a times root a equals a

body.text: There is no such rule for adding. For example, √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7, but √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. So √a + √b is not the same as √(a + b).
Simplifying surds

A perfect square is a number such as 4, 9, 16, 25 or 36, made by multiplying a whole number by itself. To simplify a surd, write the number under the root as a perfect square times another number. Use the largest perfect square you can find. Then take its square root outside.

body.title: Simplify √12, √50 and √72
steps: For √72, using 9 × 8 or 4 × 18 would leave a root that can still be simplified. Always choose the largest perfect square factor.
If Opio’s garden had sides of 6 m, the diagonal path would be √(6² + 6²) = √72 = 6√2 m, which is about 8.49 m.

body.text: Adding and subtracting surds

Like surds have the same number under the root, such as 2√3 and 5√3. You add and subtract them just as you add like terms in algebra: 2x + 5x = 7x, so 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3. Unlike surds, such as √2 and √3, cannot be combined. Sometimes you must simplify first to find like surds.
Multiplying surds and expanding brackets
Multiply the whole numbers together and the surds together. Expand brackets in the same way as in algebra, multiplying every term in one bracket by every term in the other.
Rationalising the denominator

The denominator is the bottom of a fraction. It is usual to write a fraction without a surd in the denominator. This is called rationalising the denominator. Multiply the top and the bottom by the surd. The value does not change, because you are multiplying by 1.

body.title: Rationalise 6/√3 and 1/√2
steps: Check with a calculator: 1 ÷ 1.4142… ≈ 0.7071, and 1.4142… ÷ 2 ≈ 0.7071. The two values match.

body.text: How could you put 2√3, 3√2 and √10 in order of size without a calculator? Share your method with your group and compare it with other groups.
A carpenter cutting a diagonal brace for a square frame could write its length as 5√2 cm or as 7.07 cm. When is the exact surd more useful, and when is the decimal more useful?

A surd is a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction or decimal, such as √2 or √5. Use √a × √b = √(ab) to simplify, taking out the largest perfect square. Only like surds can be added or subtracted, and to rationalise a denominator, multiply the top and bottom by the surd.
